summary.whatChanges: The accepts helper's default matcher now supports wildcard subtypes: `type/*` matches any supported value with the same main type, while `*/*` and `*` deliberately match nothing and fall through to the configured default. Candidates are sorted by quality factor and then by specificity, and the input array is no longer mutated.
behaviorChanges: An Accept header like `application/*` now resolves to a supported type such as `application/json` instead of returning the default.
`Accept: */*` (or `*` for headers like Accept-Encoding) now returns the configured default instead of matching a supported value.
When several accepted types share the same q value, more specific entries (exact > type/* > */*) are tried first, so an exact match wins over a wildcard.
The returned value is the matched entry from `supports`, not the raw header token.
The `accepts` array passed to the matcher is copied before sorting, so callers' arrays are no longer reordered in place.
risks: Treating `*/*` as a non-match diverges from common HTTP content-negotiation expectations; clients sending `Accept: */*` will get the default rather than the first supported type.
For token-based headers like Accept-Encoding/Accept-Language, a bare `*` now yields the default, which may change previously negotiated encodings.
Language tags such as `en-US` are split on `/` in matchType, so prefix wildcards only work for slash-delimited media types.
Specificity ordering only applies within equal q values, so a low-q exact match still loses to a higher-q wildcard that matches nothing.
